strengths: The paper is well-written and easy to follow.
The motivation is sound, and this is an important direction as the community increasingly moves toward fine-tuning from pre-trained models rather than training from scratch.
Framing the problem of identifying intermediate tasks as a graph search selection is both interesting and a well-founded choice.
The writing is clear and easy to follow.
The proposed method, TaCL, which leverages graph search as a curriculum for task adaptation, appears to be valid.
The idea of building task curriculum to enhance fine-tuning performance on target task is interesting.
The paper is generally well-written and easy to follow.
The target performance of TACL is better than baselines.
The paper explores the question of how to effectively select a sequence of tasks for low-resource task adaptation, a novel approach in the few-shot learning domain.
Experiments demonstrate that the task sequence selection methods outperform full fine-tuning, providing valuable insights into the transfer learning field.
The paper is clear structured and well-written.
The authors emphasize the issue of computational cost and propose several improvements to address it.
This paper is well-written and has a good motivation.
This paper investigates the challenge of adapting pre-trained models to low-resource target tasks, which is an important and interesting problem that may greatly benefit the deep learning community.
This paper formulated the task curriculum as a graph search problem, which gives a fresh perspective for transfer learning.
weaknesses: Clarify how the graph for the 6-task setting was obtained, as it is not clear whether it was generated in an almost brute-force manner where the neighbors of a node include all tasks in the graph.
A major concern is that in many domains a predetermined task graph might not be readily available.
Consider augmentation-based baselines that address data scarcity issues or use generative models like LLMs (e.g., from https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.02990).

The idea of using similar tasks and discovering task relationships is well‑studied in computer vision; please consider citing Taskonomy (http://taskonomy.stanford.edu/) and discussing the connections.
The proposed solution resembles meta‑learning but lacks a meta‑test update; discuss differences and related work such as https://arxiv.org/pdf/1911.10600.

Suggest commenting on or experimenting with anti‑curriculum learning, as studies such as https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.09533 and https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.00739 show it can sometimes outperform standard curriculum learning.

Reducing the number of training steps may not be ideal for estimating the transferability score, given deep networks can exhibit grokking behavior (https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.02177) and double descent; a comparison or discussion would be helpful.
In a resource‑constrained setting, the validation set is limited, raising doubts about the meaningfulness of heuristics that carve a portion from the training data.
There is a strong connection between TACL and continual learning; expanding related work to include connections to continual learning would strengthen the paper.
A baseline that updates only part of the network (e.g., using LoRA) is missing; exploring this experiment could reduce overfitting.

The contributions of this work are vague, as the idea of treating the task curriculum as a graph search problem is not novel; additionally, the two classic search algorithms (GBFS & MCTS) studied make the contribution rather limited.

The evaluation baselines are sparse and do not include comparisons with more advanced methods in relevant areas such as Curriculum Learning and Transfer Learning; moreover, the domains of the evaluation tasks are limited, with most experiments focused on NLP tasks and the benchmarks used not being particularly advanced.
Important details about the method are missing, making it difficult to fully understand its implementation.

Learning from a task curriculum may raise concerns about more severe forgetting and safety risks; prior research [1] shows fine‑tuning may compromise model safety, and the proposed method may exacerbate this by introducing a longer fine‑tuning path—add discussion and experiments on these aspects.

The analysis of the search results of the six‑task graph (fig 5 and fig 6) is insufficient; only the importance of a particular task (MNLI) is highlighted, leaving the effect of other tasks without discussion, making it unclear what key aspect of the task curriculum leads to performance boost.
In the related work section, the cited relevant works are generally published years ago; include more recent papers.
The main weakness of the paper is the significance and computational burden of the search algorithm.
A more simple and straightforward approach is joint learning of multiple tasks with adaptive weights, allowing multiple tasks to interact to improve performance.
Quantitative analysis of the computational burden of the proposed algorithms, compared with full‑finetuning, is needed rather than only qualitative analysis.

The paper uses two search algorithms—greedy best‑first search and Monte Carlo tree search—that are proposed by existing works, limiting novelty; the paper lacks a deep analysis of how these algorithms are adapted or modified for the task curriculum problem.

The proposed TaCL is quite similar to the existing work "Don't Stop Pretraining: Adapt Language Models to Domains and Tasks"; a more thorough analysis and comparison with it is needed, especially in the experiment section, and the paper should clearly articulate methodological and experimental differences.

The paper proposes a sequential strategy to fully exploit existing tasks; what about a parallel strategy? The paper lacks discussion on the potential benefits and drawbacks of parallel training strategies and how they might compare to the proposed sequential approach.

The proposed TaCL is much heavier than existing transfer learning methods since it has to train on several extra tasks; the paper does not provide a detailed analysis of the computational cost, which is a critical factor for practical applications—a thorough analysis of computational overhead and trade‑offs is needed.
